questions.q: What does the `Retry` field on a Task state do?
options: Automatically retries the failed state according to defined rules before giving up
Permanently disables that state from ever failing
Routes execution straight to a fallback state on the first failure
Restarts the entire state machine from StartAt
questions.explain: Retry lets a state retry itself automatically, according to ErrorEquals/IntervalSeconds/MaxAttempts/BackoffRate, before the failure is treated as unrecoverable.

questions.q: A Retry block has IntervalSeconds: 10, BackoffRate: 3.0, and MaxAttempts: 3. If the state fails every time, what are the waits before each retry attempt?
options: 10s, then 30s, then 90s
10s, then 13s, then 16s
questions.explain: BackoffRate multiplies the interval each attempt: 10s, then 10×3=30s, then 30×3=90s — exponential backoff.

questions.q: What does `Catch` do once a state's retries (if any) are exhausted and it still fails?
options: Routes the execution to a specified fallback Next state instead of letting the execution simply fail
Silently ignores the error and continues as if it succeeded
Deletes the state machine
Forces an immediate, unlimited retry loop
questions.explain: Catch is the safety net — it routes a failed state to a fallback state (e.g. one that logs or alerts), rather than the execution just stopping.

questions.q: What does `ErrorEquals: ["States.ALL"]` mean in a Catch block?
options: It's a catch-all matcher that applies to any error type
It only matches errors named literally "ALL"
It disables the Catch block
It matches only Lambda-specific errors
questions.explain: States.ALL is the wildcard error matcher — a Catch or Retry rule with it applies regardless of the specific error type raised.

questions.q: Why do production state machines typically use Retry and Catch together rather than just one?
options: Retry absorbs transient failures that often resolve on their own; Catch is the safety net for whatever still fails after retries are exhausted
ASL requires both fields to be present on every Task state
Retry and Catch do the exact same thing, so using both is redundant but harmless
Catch must always run before Retry
questions.explain: The realistic pattern is retry-then-catch: Retry quietly resolves transient blips, and Catch ensures a human or downstream alert learns about failures that don't resolve on their own.
